# Ethanol {#sec-ethanol}

Ethanol production is one of CIMS's energy-supply sub-models: it produces a low-carbon liquid fuel that the transport sector blends with gasoline. The emphasis is on the structure of the energy-service flow model — the production routes, the technologies that compete at each service, and the engineering ratios that link them. The tree is region-agnostic. Two features define the ethanol sub-model: it carries two distinct production routes — first-generation corn (grain) fermentation and second-generation cellulosic conversion — that differ markedly in carbon intensity; and, because fermentation releases a stream of nearly pure, biogenic CO₂, it is one of the cheapest places in the whole energy system to apply carbon capture, which the sub-model represents through a CCS service.

## Scope

CIMS represents the production of fuel ethanol by two routes: corn (and, in Western Canada, wheat) starch fermentation, and cellulosic conversion of crop residues and other lignocellulosic material. The sub-model covers the conversion plant and its inputs — agricultural feedstock, process steam, electricity, and a gaseous process fuel — and produces ethanol as an output that flows into the gasoline blend. Demand is set by the blending and fuel-switching choices in the consuming sectors and by renewable-fuel policy, rather than by an exogenous production target.

Adjacent activities are handled elsewhere: biodiesel has its own [Biodiesel](sector_biodiesel.qmd) chapter; gasoline is produced in [Petroleum Refining](sector_petroleum_refining.qmd); the combustion of the ethanol blend happens in the transport sectors; and feedstock cultivation is represented here only through an **Agricultural Input** service rather than the full [Agriculture](sector_agriculture.qmd) sub-model.

## Real-world context

Canadian ethanol is predominantly first-generation: corn in Eastern Canada (Ontario in particular) and wheat in the West, fermented to ethanol and blended into gasoline under the federal Clean Fuel Regulations and provincial renewable-content mandates [@nrcan-ethanol]. Cellulosic ethanol — made from crop residues, wood, and other lignocellulosic feedstock — is a second-generation technology that is much less developed but carries a substantially lower carbon intensity, because it is not burdened by the cultivation emissions (fertiliser N₂O, farm diesel, land use) of a dedicated grain crop and uses material that would otherwise decay or be burned [@cen-ethanol].

The sector has one striking decarbonisation feature. The fermentation step that turns sugars into ethanol releases roughly an equal mass of CO₂, and that CO₂ is biogenic and almost pure — it needs little separation before it can be compressed and stored. This makes ethanol plants among the lowest-cost carbon-capture opportunities anywhere, and capturing biogenic fermentation CO₂ delivers net-negative emissions (BECCS). The CIMS structure reflects both points: it separates the corn and cellulosic routes, carries life-cycle CO₂, CH₄, and N₂O accounting through the feedstock and process services, and provides a **CCS** service the routes can draw on.

## Model structure

The sub-model divides into a **Product** sub-tree — the two production routes — and a **Service** sub-tree of the inputs they draw on. @fig-ethanol-flow-model shows the structure. Each node carries a competition rule (see @sec-technology-competition); the production chains are fixed-ratio sequences and the technology choices occur at the service leaves.

![Energy-service flow model of the ethanol sub-model. Two production routes — Corn (grain fermentation) and Cellulosic — convert feedstock into ethanol, drawing on an Agricultural Input service, process Steam, a gaseous Methane Fuel supply, electricity, and a shared CCS service well suited to the pure biogenic CO₂ from fermentation; life-cycle CO₂, CH₄, and N₂O are tracked.](images/ethanol_flow_model.svg){#fig-ethanol-flow-model .lightbox width=90%}

### Products: corn and cellulosic routes

- **Corn** — first-generation starch fermentation. It draws on the **Agricultural Input** service (the grain feedstock and its cultivation energy) and on **Steam** for cooking, distillation, and drying, and is the more steam-intensive of the two routes.
- **Cellulosic** — second-generation conversion of lignocellulosic feedstock (crop residues, wood). In the model it draws less on the agricultural-cultivation input and instead consumes some industrial diesel for feedstock handling, plus **Steam**; its lower cultivation burden gives it a lower life-cycle carbon intensity.

### Services: feedstock, heat, fuel, and capture

- **Agricultural Input** — feedstock cultivation, competing diesel-powered, efficient-diesel, and biodiesel-powered farming, so the energy and emissions of growing the grain are represented (including the option to displace farm diesel with biodiesel).
- **Steam** — process heat, competing natural-gas, coal, and electric boilers, cogeneration, and CCS-equipped variants.
- **Methane Fuel** — the gaseous-fuel supply, competing natural gas against biogas, biomass gasification, and hydrogen.
- **CCS** — the shared carbon-capture service, especially valuable here because of the pure fermentation CO₂.

## Decarbonisation technologies

Ethanol decarbonisation means lowering life-cycle carbon intensity — shifting toward cellulosic feedstock, cleaning up process energy, and, distinctively, capturing the pure fermentation CO₂ for net-negative emissions. @tbl-ethanol-decarb summarises maturity and @tbl-ethanol-cost gives indicative costs.

| Technology | Indicative benefit | Maturity |
|:-----|:--------|:----|
| Fermentation CO₂ capture (BECCS) | Captures near-pure biogenic CO₂; net-negative | Early commercial (low-cost capture) |
| Cellulosic route (vs corn) | Much lower life-cycle CI; avoids cultivation burden | Pilot / early commercial |
| Biodiesel-powered / efficient farming | Lowers feedstock-cultivation emissions | Commercial |
| Electric process steam / boilers | Removes fossil process-heat CO₂ | Commercial |
| Biogas / biomass-gas / hydrogen process fuel | Decarbonises gaseous process fuel | Commercial / emerging |
| CCS on process steam | Captures process-heat CO₂ | Demonstration |

: Indicative performance and maturity of key ethanol decarbonisation options {#tbl-ethanol-decarb}

The cost estimates in @tbl-ethanol-cost are order-of-magnitude figures from public literature [@nrcan-ethanol; @cen-ethanol], expressed in 2025 Canadian dollars (US-dollar sources converted at roughly 1.37 CAD/USD and adjusted to 2025). They are indicative, for relative comparison rather than budgeting, and are separate from the values the model carries internally.

| Decarbonisation option | Capex | Operating cost / cost of CO₂ | Energy / CI effect |
|:-----|:-----|:-----|:-----|
| Fermentation CO₂ capture (BECCS) | low (compression, dehydration only) | ~CAD 25–60 / t CO₂ (cheapest industrial capture) | net-negative; near-pure CO₂ |
| Cellulosic conversion (vs corn) | higher than corn plant | feedstock-dependent | much lower life-cycle CI |
| Electric process boiler | ~150–400 CAD/kWth | electricity-priced heat | removes process-heat fossil CO₂ |
| Biomass / biogas process fuel | ~800–1,400 CAD/kWth (biomass) | low-carbon fuel | decarbonises process heat |
| CCS on process steam | +30–50% on boiler plant | ~CAD 100–200 / t CO₂ | captures process CO₂ |

: Indicative techno-economic characteristics of ethanol decarbonisation options, 2025 CAD {#tbl-ethanol-cost}

### Capturing fermentation CO₂ (the cheapest BECCS)

The standout option is capturing the fermentation CO₂. Unlike a flue gas, it emerges nearly pure, so only compression and dehydration are needed before storage — capture costs are a small fraction of those for dilute industrial streams. Because the carbon is biogenic, storing it yields net-negative emissions. The model represents this through the **CCS** service; given the cost advantage, it is the single most valuable lever in the sub-model.

### Feedstock and process energy

Shifting from corn to cellulosic feedstock lowers the cultivation burden, and within the corn route the **Agricultural Input** options (efficient or biodiesel-powered farming) reduce field emissions. On the plant side, switching **Steam** to electric, biomass, or biogas, or adding CCS to gas-fired steam, cuts the conversion footprint — the same low-carbon heat options described in the [Low-Temperature Industrial Heat](low_temp_industrial_heat.qmd) chapter.

## Economics

Technology choice at every tech-compete node follows the lifecycle-cost competition of @sec-technology-competition. Each technology carries a capital cost, fixed operating and maintenance cost, an output basis, service requests for the inputs it consumes, and availability and lifetime years; these are annualised, combined with service costs into a lifecycle cost, and converted to market shares by the inverse-power choice rule.

Ethanol technologies are discounted at rates of roughly 10–40% in the current data. As elsewhere in CIMS these are **behavioural** (revealed or empirical) discount rates rather than true financial costs of capital, capturing the payback horizons and adoption barriers that govern real investment decisions; CIMS applies this rate throughout the lifecycle-cost calculation, as set out in the discount-rate discussion of the [Theory](theory.qmd) chapter and in @sec-technology-competition. **Heterogeneity (variance) parameters** are set around 10–25 across the competitions.

As with biodiesel, the emissions accounting is **life-cycle**: the sub-model carries CO₂, CH₄, and N₂O factors so that agricultural N₂O, process CH₄, and CO₂ are all represented, and the net benefit of ethanol emerges from the difference between these emissions and the gasoline it displaces. The **CCS** service applies an emissions-removal factor to the routes that request it — and because the captured fermentation CO₂ is biogenic, that removal can drive the route's net emissions below zero. The carbon price therefore rewards the cellulosic route, clean process energy, and above all fermentation-CO₂ capture.

## Regional coverage and differences

All seven modelled regions — Alberta, the Atlantic region, British Columbia, Manitoba, Ontario, Québec, and Saskatchewan — carry both the corn and cellulosic routes. In practice corn ethanol is concentrated in Ontario and the East, wheat-based grain ethanol in the Prairies, and cellulosic feedstock potential follows crop-residue and forestry availability. Regional differences show up in feedstock mix and in the carbon intensity of the grid supplying process electricity.

## Limitations and planned extensions

The ethanol sub-model is compact and supply-side. Its main limitations: it treats feedstock through a single Agricultural Input service rather than linking to the agriculture sub-model; it applies a single CCS cost rather than recognising the unusually cheap fermentation-CO₂ capture; and its corn/cellulosic split and intensities are inherited from older calibrations. The TODOs above record these priorities, of which making the cheap fermentation-CO₂ BECCS pathway explicit is the most consequential for emissions outcomes.
